analysis.one_liner: Expands Medicaid and children's health coverage to low-income parents, legal immigrants, and Native Americans and funds minority health programs.
analysis.headline: A Senate bill with 19 Democratic sponsors that would have extended public health coverage to low-income parents, legal immigrants, and Native Americans was referred to the Finance Committee and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have let states cover low-income parents and pregnant women through the children's health insurance program (SCHIP, renamed FamilyCare), given states the option to cover everyone under the poverty line through Medicaid, restored Medicaid and SCHIP eligibility for legal immigrants, and locked in guaranteed funding for the Indian Health Service. It also funded interpreter services, safety-net clinics, minority health research, and efforts to diversify the health workforce. It died in committee without a hearing or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income parents and pregnant women whose children are enrolled in Medicaid or SCHIP, adults under the poverty line in states that opt in, legal immigrants cut off from these programs by the 1996 welfare law, Native Americans and Alaska Natives who rely on chronically underfunded Indian Health Service facilities, patients with limited English, and safety-net hospitals and community clinics that treat the uninsured.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low-income families, legal immigrants, Native Americans

how_it_helps.text: Creates an optional FamilyCare category so states can cover parents and pregnant women up to their children's income levels, with $2 billion per year in new federal allotments for 2006-2007 and $3 billion per year for 2008-2009, plus a higher federal matching rate for states that participate.

Lets states cover all residents with family income at or below the poverty line through Medicaid, and repeals the 1996-law restrictions that bar many legal immigrants from Medicaid and SCHIP for their first five years in the country.

Guarantees Indian Health Service clinical funding by formula each year — roughly 390 percent of fiscal 2002 obligations, adjusted per patient and indexed to medical inflation — instead of relying on annual appropriations, and makes the service patients not liable for charges on authorized contract care.

Requires federal reimbursement for interpreter and translation services under Medicare, Medicaid, and SCHIP, and funds grants, workforce scholarships, and data collection aimed at closing racial and ethnic gaps in health outcomes.

Creates a Health Safety Net Infrastructure Trust Fund, loan guarantees, and grants for public hospitals, community health centers, and clinics that disproportionately treat minority and uninsured patients.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through roughly $10 billion in new FamilyCare allotments over four years plus guaranteed Indian Health Service funding, and state taxpayers, through the state share of any Medicaid expansions states elect to make.

drawbacks.text: The bill authorizes substantial new federal spending — $2 billion per year in 2006 and 2007 and $3 billion per year in 2008 and 2009 for FamilyCare alone, plus automatic Indian Health Service funding outside the normal appropriations process — which opponents would weigh against deficit concerns.
Coverage expansions are optional for states, so gains would be uneven across the country and depend on each state's willingness to put up matching funds.

The bill creates numerous new commissions, offices, working groups, and studies — including a National Commission for Expanded Access to Health Care and a Minority Health and Genomics Commission — whose cost and usefulness critics could question.
Extending Medicaid and SCHIP to recent legal immigrants reverses a deliberate restriction in the 1996 welfare law, a policy choice opponents defended at the time on fiscal and immigration grounds.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core tradeoff is straightforward: a large, multi-year public investment in health coverage for uninsured low-income families, immigrants, and Native Americans, paid for by federal and state taxpayers. The coverage and Indian Health Service funding provisions are concrete and targeted; the many new offices and commissions add administrative overhead with less certain payoff. Because nearly every expansion is a state option, the bill's real-world effect would have varied widely by state.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee in July 2005, the committee never acted on it, and it expired when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Sen. Daniel Akaka introduced the Healthcare Equality and Accountability Act on July 29, 2005, joined on introduction by 15 other Democratic senators including Reid, Kennedy, Obama, and Clinton.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance on July 29, 2005.
The committee took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote is recorded — and Akaka's only later activity was introductory remarks in February 2006.
The bill never received a floor vote in either chamber and died when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained coverage. The bill died quietly in committee without a vote, so no senator or committee had to go on record against it; opponents of expanded public health spending and the status quo prevailed by default, while uninsured low-income families got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Uninsured families gained nothing; the bill died quietly in committee

for.name: Sen. Daniel Akaka
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor twice, in July 2005 and February 2006.

for.name: Sens. Reid, Durbin, Bingaman, Corzine, Murray, Kennedy, Landrieu, Lautenberg, Inouye, Pryor, Mikulski, Obama, Dodd, Lieberman, and Clinton
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors when the bill was introduced on July 29, 2005.

for.name: 18 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill after introduction, bringing total cosponsorship to 18, all Democrats.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of referral under Sen. Charles Grassley (R-IA), chair
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on July 29, 2005 and took no recorded action on it — no hearing, markup, or vote — for the remaining 17 months of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 19 senators associated with the bill were Democrats, and the Republican-controlled Senate Finance Committee never acted on it, so the fight tracked party lines even though no vote was ever taken.

industries.industry: Safety-net health providers (public hospitals, community health centers, clinics)
industries.note: The bill creates a Health Safety Net Infrastructure Trust Fund, loan guarantees, and capital grants for facilities that disproportionately treat minority and uninsured patients. Ordinary people benefit as patients when these facilities are financially stable.

industries.industry: Indian Health Service and tribal health programs
industries.note: Guaranteed annual funding, payment-timeliness rules, and reestablishment of the IHS as a Public Health Service agency would have ended reliance on year-to-year discretionary funding. Native communities and the providers who serve them both gain.

industries.industry: Health insurers and Medicaid managed-care plans
industries.note: Coverage expansions under Medicaid and FamilyCare would add enrolled lives, much of it delivered through managed-care contracts. The bill expands public programs rather than routing new subsidies through private insurance, so the entrenchment is modest.

New entitlement spending of $2-3 billion per year for FamilyCare plus automatic Indian Health Service funding would be paid from the Treasury; in a bill of this kind the taxpayers' cost is the mirror image of the public's coverage gain.
